szoveg_eredeti:
Integrative Structural Modeling Combines Artificial Intelligence and Tomography for Macromolecular Assemblies

Integrative structural modeling has emerged as a cornerstone methodology for determining the three-dimensional architectures of large macromolecular assemblies that remain resistant to conventional experimental determination alone. By integrating data obtained across multiple distinct experimental techniques with physical principles, statistical analysis of previously solved structures, and computational predictions, this hybrid paradigm overcomes the inherent spatial and physical limitations of individual structural tools. A modern resurgence of enthusiasm for integrative modeling has been ignited by rapid, concurrent breakthroughs across computational biology and experimental biophysics, specifically the emergence of artificial intelligence frameworks capable of predicting protein structures alongside hardware and software advancements in cellular cryo-electron microscopy. Within this evolving framework, theoretical predictions generated by deep learning tools can be incorporated directly into experimental density maps, maximizing accuracy, precision, completeness, and experimental efficiency when resolving assemblies operating directly within their cellular contexts.

The foundational framework of integrative structure determination relies on assembling disparate experimental data types spanning a wide spectrum of spatial resolutions. High-resolution structural information obtained from X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and deep learning algorithms like AlphaFold can be systematically unified with lower-resolution topological observations. These lower-resolution data sources include density maps derived from electron cryo-microscopy, in situ cryo-electron tomography volumes, chemical crosslinks measured through mass spectrometry, small-angle X-ray scattering curves, Förster resonance energy transfer distances, and even genetic interaction measurements recorded in living cells. To assimilate these heterogeneous measurements, computational platforms apply rigorous statistical formulations, particularly Bayesian inference frameworks, which formally account for experimental noise and measurement uncertainties while evaluating candidate structural configurations. This probabilistic assembly ensures that generated structural architectures satisfy physical restraints and experimental observations without being disproportionately biased by artifacts present within any single methodology.

Several computational platforms have been established to execute multi-scale and multi-state integrative modeling workflows. Chief among these is the Integrative Modeling Platform, an open-source architecture that optimizes scoring functions and spatial sampling parameters to reconcile diverse experimental inputs into consistent conformational ensembles. Complementary methods include Assembline, which couples rigid-body fitting into medium-resolution electron microscopy volumes with molecular visualization and sampling routines to accelerate the assembly of sprawling multi-subunit complexes. For atomistic docking, the High Ambiguity Driven DOCKing platform translates experimental observations from mutagenesis, nuclear magnetic resonance, chemical crosslinking, and scattering experiments into ambiguous interaction restraints, supporting the characterization of assemblies composed of up to twenty macromolecules. Additionally, specialized flexible fitting methods, such as molecular dynamics flexible fitting and responsibility-based flexible fitting through TEMPy-REFF, refine known atomic coordinates iteratively within experimental density maps using energetic biasing potentials or expectation-maximization algorithms.

The practical utility of integrative structural modeling is prominently demonstrated by recent structural elucidations of intricate cellular machines, most notably the nuclear pore complex. Spanning the double membrane of the nuclear envelope to govern nucleocytoplasmic transport, this massive architecture has been dissected through the combination of medium-resolution cryo-electron tomography, single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, chemical crosslinking mass spectrometry, quantitative fluorescence imaging, and AlphaFold structural models. Recent integrative models have resolved the molecular organization of the cytoplasmic ring, the cytoplasmic face, the linker-scaffold network, and the nuclear basket, while detailing the spatial functions of specific nucleoporins such as Nup38, the cytoplasmic filament nucleoporin complex, and Pom153. Crucially, whole-pore integrative reconstructions have documented functional transitions between dilated and constricted conformations of the inner ring, capturing the structural plasticity and physical robustness required to facilitate selective macromolecular transport across the nuclear boundary.

Beyond the nuclear pore complex, integrative structural modeling has successfully revealed the functional architectures of key chromatin-modifying machines and specialized intercellular adhesion junctions. Structural investigations of the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase complex brought together negative-stain and cryo-electron microscopy reconstructions, X-ray crystallography, chemical crosslinking, nuclear magnetic resonance, mass spectrometry, and homology modeling to delineate three essential subcomplexes. This integrative structure established how the methyl-CpG-binding domain protein adopts distinct states, employing an extended disordered segment to physically bridge the chromatin remodeling and deacetylase enzymatic modules. Similarly, integrative analysis resolved the molecular arrangement of the desmosomal outer dense plaque, which anchors intermediate filaments in tissues exposed to mechanical tension. By synthesizing cryo-electron tomography, immuno-electron microscopy, crystallography, yeast two-hybrid assays, binding assays, and sequence-based predictions, researchers localized disordered segments of plakophilin and plakoglobin, revealing novel protein interaction interfaces that explain junctional assembly.

A primary methodological challenge highlighted across these large-scale assemblies is the pervasive presence of intrinsically disordered proteins and flexible protein regions. Unlike globular proteins that fold into stable, well-defined tertiary geometries in their monomeric states, intrinsically disordered proteins exist as dynamic, interconverting conformational ensembles in thermodynamic equilibrium. These disordered segments constitute a substantial fraction of eukaryotic proteomes and execute vital cellular roles, including forming the selective permeability barrier in nuclear pore complexes through disordered FG-nucleoporins. However, their structural heterogeneity prevents conventional static structural characterization. While protein language models have emerged as powerful tools for sequence-based representation learning, standard models remain inherently biased toward folded proteins and fail to capture transient interactions, dynamic conformational shifts, or environmental context. Expanding representation learning to incorporate structural priors, physics-based constraints, and specialized tuning on disordered sequences remains essential for accurately describing these dynamic molecules.

Generating realistic conformational ensembles of disordered proteins requires sophisticated computational sampling techniques that overcome the limitations of standard molecular dynamics simulations. Traditional molecular dynamics force fields parameterized for globular proteins frequently overestimate compactness or fail to reproduce experimental dimensions for disordered chains, prompting ongoing development of specialized force fields and revised water-protein interaction potentials.
